title: Why You Cannot Believe Your Way Into Learning
author: Hendrick, Carl
summary: For most people, the hardest thing to understand about learning is that the strategies which work in the short term often feel like failure, while the ones that pay off in the future often feel like success in the present. A new paper in Educational Psychology Review applies this uncomfortable truth to the most popular intervention in modern education, growth mindset, and finds it wanting: as a standalone treatment it produces effects on achievement that are vanishingly small and disappear entirely under proper scrutiny. Growth Mindset strategies require little that is uncomfortable of teacher or pupil, which is exactly the type of idea that spreads regardless of whether it works. Belief only governs whether a student perseveres; but it cannot tell them what to persevere at, so they often persevere at ineffective habits they already prefer. However, the strategies that actually lead to learning such as retrieval practice and spacing, feel worse and therefore are not as popular. Despite this, every parent and teacher knows that motivation and belief matters greatly. A child's conviction that she can improve does little on its own, but can do a great deal when it is supported by good mentoring and a genuine sense of belonging: the conditions that make her feel secure enough to bear the initial discomfort real learning demands. There is a story I have probably repeated a little too often about Niels Bohr who was visited by a friend after winning the Nobel prize for his model of the atom. The friend, after seeing a lucky horseshoe over his door, asked him why an eminent man of rationality and reason would have a superstitious symbol over his door? Bohr replied that of course he didnt believe that it works, but that he was told that it works even if you don't believe in it. The growth mindset poster in schools is education equivalent of Bohr's horseshoe. Most teachers instinctively know that showing children a video about brain plasticity, or telling them that mistakes help them grow, or adding 'yet' to a negative sentence, will not by itself make them better readers or help them solve quadratic equations. And yet we keep hanging them anyway, because the alternative, admitting we do not have a quick fix for how children learn, is far less comforting than a slogan on the wall. The idea of a growth mindset remains one of the most successful ideas education has ever seen. It is short, intuitive, cheap, and almost too good to be true; an intervention can be delivered in as little as ten minutes through an online module, and it leaves both teacher and pupil feeling that something transformative has occurred. In a new paper, Anne Cleary and Daniel Robinson place it alongside learning styles and grit, in a small family of concepts that are quick to grasp, relatively easy to administer, and almost entirely resistant to disconfirmation or falsification. They borrow a useful term for this from Sinatra and Jacobson: the zombie concept , an idea that no amount of evidence can kill, because it keeps rising again merely on the strength of how right it feels. However, there is a real dimension to growth mindset so why does it endure in its ineffective motivational poster form? And what does it tell us about how education chooses its ideas? What the evidence actually says The empirical picture is now difficult to argue with. Macnamara and Burgoyne's meta-analysis found a mean effect of growth mindset training on academic achievement of d = 0.05; once you correct for publication bias, that already negligible figure falls to somewhere between 0.01 and 0.03, which is to say nothing at all. The result holds up under the most reasonable stress tests. When the authors restricted their analysis to studies in which the intervention demonstrably shifted students' mindsets in the intended direction, the effect on performance vanished. When they restricted it again to the handful of studies meeting basic methodological standards, it vanished a second time. This is not the verdict of a single hostile study either. Foliano and colleagues ran a randomised controlled trial across more than a hundred English schools and over five thousand pupils, and found no advantage for those who received the training. Bahnik and Vranka found no relationship between growth mindset and admission test scores among more than five thousand Czech applicants. And the studies that do report glowing results tend, on inspection, to often be correlational: Claro and Loeb's much cited 2024 paper , which announced that students with a growth mindset learn more in school, can establish only that the two travel together, not that one produces Slogans are usually nonsense but I like this because it tells a child that the discomfort she is about to feel is not a sign that something has gone wrong, but the price of the thing going right; that the path which feels worst in the moment is often the one that pays off later. This is not motivation in the familiar sense; it is honesty about the structure of learning. A slogan that tells children how easy initial learning ought to feel is simply dishonest. And we should be honest with children about how learning happens. Does the causal arrow point the other way? There is I think, a structural reason why standalone therapeutic interventions like this dont work and it's not because 'we've never tried growth mindset properly." Suppose the training succeeds perfectly; suppose a child walks out genuinely persuaded that her intelligence is malleable and that effort will pay. What, precisely, is she meant to do next? Belief governs whether she persists but tells them nothing about what she should be persisting at. A student convinced of her own brain plasticity but left to her own devices will simply persist harder at the ineffective strategies she already favours: re-reading, highlighting, the comfortable rituals of revision that feel like work and accomplish little. You cannot believe your way into knowing how to study, any more than you can believe your way into knowing how to swim. Motivation does not reliably produce achievement; but achievement often produces motivation. Self-belief is far more often the consequence of competence than its cause. Prepare a child to deliver a genuinely good speech, one built through explicit instruction, modelling, specific feedback,rehearsal, and caring mentorship and support, and you will have done more for her sense of her own capabilities than any number of assemblies about the plasticity of the brain or videos of Michael Jordan failing 99 times but then succeeding once. You cannot instil the feeling that competence produces, while completely skipping the actual competence. Mentorship, motivation and belonging One person who I think has thought about this better than most is David Yeager, who arrived at a version of the same conclusion long before the latest meta-analyses. I have written before about his important work on 'stealth interventions' and his work since the National Study of Learning Mindsets rests on the argument that belief moves achievement only where the surrounding context affords the behaviour it recommends. The intervention can change what a student thinks while changing nothing about what she does, unless peers and teachers already reward the seeking of challenge. He presents this as a defence of mindset, but it is closer to a concession I think, because it grants the structural point precisely: belief is inert without a vehicle to carry it. Yeager argues that the near-zero averages in the meta-analyses are misleading, an artefact of pooling the contexts in which the effect is real with the many in which it is absent; the effects are heterogeneous, they argue, not absent. Grant them this entirely, and the case against the classroom product is stronger, because if belief pays off solely where the environment is already supportive, then the universal, context-blind deployment, the module, the assembly, the laminated poster, is exactly the condition under which the research predicts nothing will happen. The most authoritative case for mindset turns out to question the version that many schools were actually sold. What remains is not a disagreement about whether belief needs a complement, but about which one: Cleary and Robinson would attach retrieval practice; Yeager would attach a supportive context and the deliberate pursuit of difficulty. It is telling, too, where Yeager has since taken his thinking. His recent work has migrated from the growth mindset, a belief lodged inside the student, to what he calls the mentor mindset, a stance adopted by the adult: high standards paired with the support that makes meeting them possible. He sets it against two failure modes a teacher will recognise instantly, the enforcer who demands rigour without any help, and the protector who offers warmth while quietly lowering the bar. His exemplar is a physics teacher who sets genuinely hard problems, refuses to simply hand over the answer, scaffolds the task until students can attempt it, and lets them revise when they get it wrong. This dovetails nicely I think with Jon Hutchinson 's thoughtful work on belonging . You cannot do belonging, Hutchinson argues, any more than you can believe your way into learning; it is earned by a child actually doing something that counts as membership of the group. A great point he makes is that the harder you push a child academically, the more her sense of belonging matters, because difficult material makes her struggle, and struggle is exactly what prompts the anxious question of whether she belongs here at all; a question that depletes the very cognitive resources the work requires. I like both these ideas because they are really the support that makes difficulty bearable, and so makes rigour possible. Dweck deserves great respect
